title: Advanced ways of talking about the future
tagline: Official, imminent, inevitable or just polite — English keeps a different future for each.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 1 — multiple-choice cloze (be to / due to / bound to / verge of)
Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (TO, DUE, BOUND, VERGE, HAVE)
Writing Part 1 — formal proposal or report: announcing plans and schedules
Speaking Part 3 — negotiating and making polite offers and suggestions
why: General English gives you going to and will; C1 English needs to sound like a press release, a timetable, a worried friend and a polite host, sometimes within the same paragraph. Use of English tests these forms precisely because each one commits the speaker to a different degree of certainty and formality, and Writing Part 1 rewards a report that announces plans without repeating will in every sentence.

formula.chip: be to / be about to / be due to / be bound to / be on the verge of
formula.ex: is due to / is about to

head: Pattern
Meaning
Example
rows: be to + infinitive
a formal, official arrangement
the minister is to visit the school next week
be about to + infinitive
happening in the next few moments
the plane is about to take off
be due to + infinitive
scheduled for a specific time
the results are due to be published on Friday
be bound to + infinitive
certain to happen, given the circumstances
with that much talent, she is bound to succeed
be on the verge of + -ing
right at the point of happening
the talks are on the verge of collapsing
future continuous
a routine future event, or a polite assumption
will be arriving around nine; Will you be needing the hall?
future perfect continuous
a duration completed by a future point
by June, she will have been working here for five years
shall (formal)
offers and suggestions, first person
Shall we begin? / Shall I fetch the results?

use.point: Imminent and near-certain futures: about to, on the verge of, bound to

examples.text: The keynote speaker is about to take the stage.
Talks between the two schools are on the verge of breaking down completely.
examples.note: on the verge of + -ing = right at the point of happening

examples.text: Given her results this term, Nadia is bound to come top of the class.
examples.note: bound to = certain, based on the evidence

use.point: Official and scheduled futures: be to, be due to

examples.text: The Minister of Education is to open the new science block on Thursday.
examples.note: be to = a formal, official arrangement

examples.text: The bus is due to leave at exactly 7.15, not a minute later.

use.point: Future continuous for routine plans, politeness and assumption; will for assumption and habit

examples.text: Don't worry about a lift — I'll be passing your street anyway.
examples.note: future continuous softens an offer as something already arranged

examples.text: Will you be needing the projector this afternoon, Mr Ramos?
examples.note: a polite enquiry, assuming a routine plan rather than asking a favour

examples.text: That will be the courier at the door — he's always this punctual.
examples.note: will for a confident assumption about the present

examples.text: Left alone for five minutes, the twins will argue about absolutely anything.
examples.note: will for a typical, predictable habit

use.point: Future perfect continuous and shall in formal contexts

examples.text: By December, the choir will have been rehearsing this programme for eight months.
examples.note: duration completed by a future point

examples.text: Shall we reconvene at half past two?
examples.note: shall for a formal, first-person suggestion

watch_out.wrong: The ceremony is to starting at noon.
watch_out.right: The ceremony is to start at noon.
watch_out.why: Be to is followed by the bare infinitive, not the -ing form.

watch_out.wrong: Hurry, the train is on the verge to leave!
watch_out.right: Hurry, the train is on the verge of leaving!
watch_out.why: Be on the verge of is followed by a gerund introduced by of, not to.

watch_out.wrong: With that talent, she is bound succeed.
watch_out.right: With that talent, she is bound to succeed.
watch_out.why: Be bound to needs the infinitive with to.

watch_out.wrong: Will you needing the hall this evening?
watch_out.right: Will you be needing the hall this evening?
watch_out.why: The polite, assumption use of will needs the continuous form, not the bare present.

watch_out.wrong: By Friday, the team will finish the project for two weeks.
watch_out.right: By Friday, the team will have been working on the project for two weeks.
watch_out.why: A duration completed by a future point needs the future perfect continuous, not the future simple.

watch_out.wrong: Shall he collect the certificates tomorrow?
watch_out.why: In modern formal English, shall for offers and suggestions is almost always first person.

dialogue.title: Opening day
dialogue.context: The class makes last-minute preparations before the mayor officially opens the school's new library, and things almost go wrong.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Right, everyone — the mayor is to officially open the new library tomorrow morning.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Is he definitely coming? Politicians cancel all the time.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: He confirmed yesterday. The ceremony is due to start at nine sharp.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Look outside — the delivery van is on the verge of reversing straight into the gate!

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Someone stop him! He's about to hit the new sign.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Phew, that was close. Honestly, with this much chaos, something is bound to go wrong tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Don't jinx it. Now, will you all be wearing your uniforms for the photos?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Of course. And by the time the mayor arrives, the whole class will have been setting up chairs for two hours.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Typical. Knowing our luck, it will rain right when the ribbon gets cut.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Shall we check the sound system one more time, just to be safe?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good idea. And Mateo — will you be bringing the spare microphone, just in case?

items.sentence: The final whistle blows any second — the referee ___ end the match.
items.why: be about to = happening in the next few moments

items.sentence: According to the timetable, the ferry ___ depart at exactly 6 pm.
With three trophies already this season, the team ___ win the league.
items.why: be bound to = certain, given the evidence

items.sentence: The Queen ___ unveil the new wing of the museum next spring, according to the official programme.
items.why: be to = a formal, official arrangement

items.sentence: ___ you be needing any help with the boxes?
items.why: polite future continuous, not a direct request

items.sentence: By the time we land, we ___ flying for over fourteen hours.
items.why: future perfect continuous for a duration completed by a future point

items.sentence: ___ I open a window? It's rather warm in here.
items.why: shall for a formal, first-person offer

summary: The near future runs from on the verge of (this instant) through about to and due to (scheduled) to bound to (certain, but not yet fixed).
Be to and be due to belong to official, scheduled or programmed events — timetables, ceremonies, announcements.
The future continuous can soften a plan into something already arranged, which is why it sounds more polite than will for offers and requests.
Will also expresses a confident assumption about the present, or a predictable habit — not only a decision about the future.
Shall survives in formal English mainly for first-person offers and suggestions: Shall I…? / Shall we…?
